nameStory: Micrasterias laticeps gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'small star' (micro + asterias) and 'broad head' (lati + ceps), describing its distinctive star-like shape with wide, flattened lobes. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, scientists sometimes call it the 'broad-headed star desmid' for its characteristic appearance. This tiny aquatic organism is actually a single-celled algae that looks like an intricate living snowflake!
description: Micrasterias laticeps is a microscopic single-celled green algae that lives in freshwater ponds and lakes throughout New England. Despite being invisible to the naked eye, each cell is a masterpiece of natural architecture, shaped like a flattened star with broad, rounded lobes extending from a central constriction. The entire organism is typically only about 150-200 micrometers across (that's smaller than the period at the end of this sentence!). You'll need a microscope to see these beautiful geometric creatures, but they're worth the effort for their stunning symmetrical design.

idTips.label: Star-shaped symmetry
idTips.description: The cell has a distinctive bilateral symmetry with broad, flattened lobes that extend outward like points of a star, each lobe wider at the tip than at the base

idTips.label: Central constriction
idTips.description: A clear narrow 'waist' or constriction divides the cell into two identical halves, creating an hourglass-like silhouette when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Smooth margins
idTips.description: The outer edges of the lobes are relatively smooth and rounded rather than deeply notched or spiny like some relatives

idTips.label: Green chloroplasts
idTips.description: Bright green plate-like structures (chloroplasts) are arranged in radiating patterns within each half of the cell, visible as distinct green bands

idTips.label: Rigid cell wall
idTips.description: The cell maintains its precise geometric shape due to a firm cellulose wall that doesn't flex or bend when the organism moves

habitat: Micrasterias laticeps thrives in clean, slightly acidic freshwater environments like mountain ponds, bog pools, and pristine lakes throughout New England's higher elevations. Look for them in soft-water habitats with low mineral content, often associated with sphagnum moss and other acid-loving plants. They're particularly common in the Adirondack region of New York and similar environments in Vermont and New Hampshire's White Mountains.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as ice melts and water temperatures rise, though you'll need to collect water samples and examine them microscopically to observe them.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when reproduction is most active - this is the best time to find specimens in pond water samples.
seasonality.fall: Numbers remain stable through early fall, and the cooler temperatures may actually make specimens easier to observe as they move more slowly.
seasonality.winter: Populations survive under ice in a dormant state, though they're much less active and harder to locate in water samples.

funFact: Each Micrasterias cell is actually two identical halves joined together - when it reproduces, each half grows a completely new matching partner, like biological photocopying, ensuring every generation maintains the same perfect geometric design that has remained unchanged for millions of years!
confusionNotes: Micrasterias species can be tricky to tell apart without careful measurement, but M. laticeps is distinguished by its broader, less deeply divided lobes compared to the more intricately cut M. pinnatifida or the more rounded M. rotata. Remember: 'laticeps' means broad-headed, so look for those wide, paddle-like lobe tips.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'algae,' desmids like Micrasterias are quite different from the slimy green algae most people know - they're single-celled organisms that belong to a group more closely related to land plants than to typical pond scum. The beautiful geometric patterns have made them favorites among microscopists for over 150 years.
compareHints: Micrasterias laticeps differs from its relatives by having broader, less divided lobes - M. truncata has more angular, cut-off edges, while M. pinnatifida has deeply divided, fern-like lobes. M. rotata is more circular overall, lacking the broad paddle-shaped extensions that give laticeps its distinctive wide-headed appearance.
